Russian folklore encompasses the mythology, fairy tales, folk customs, and carnival traditions of Russian culture stretching back centuries. Rich with magical creatures, transformations, and archetypal heroes, these narratives drew on Slavic paganism, Byzantine influences, and the experiences of Russian peasant life. The tradition became a vital source for modernist artists, particularly composers and choreographers seeking authentic, emotionally resonant material.

Central to Russian folklore are magical creatures. Baba Yaga is a fearsome witch. Firebirds appear throughout the traditions. There are various mythological beings drawn from pre-Christian Slavic belief systems. These creatures represent forces of transformation and power.

Russian carnival traditions, particularly the Maslenitsa or butter festival, featured puppet theater, music, and masked performance that influenced later ballet narratives. These celebrations were central to Russian popular culture. The Firebird, known as Zhar-ptica, appears in numerous Russian fairy tales as a magical bird of gold or fire, embodying transformation and transcendence. Petrushka, also called Punch, originates in Russian carnival puppet theater, representing the clever fool figure who subverts authority through wit and mischief.

Russian fairy tales, or skazki, typically follow archetypal patterns. There is a humble hero. There are magical helpers. There are impossible tasks. Resolution comes through cunning or virtue. These patterns create the distinctive feel of Russian narrative traditions.

The tradition draws significantly from both Slavic pagan mythology and Orthodox Christian values, creating a unique synthesis. This blending of pagan and Christian elements is distinctive to Russian culture. Early-twentieth-century Russian artists including Stravinsky and Fokine revived folklore as a source of authentic modernity. They rejected western European refinement in favor of the raw power of folk traditions.

Petrushka is the ballet grounded in Russian carnival puppet traditions and folk narrative. The Firebird is based on the famous Russian fairy tale character of mystical transformation. Igor Stravinsky was the composer who drew on Russian folklore for The Firebird, Petrushka, and Le Sacre du Printemps. Michel Fokine was the choreographer who integrated Russian folk traditions into modernist ballet aesthetics.

The Russian Empire was the cultural and political context that preserved and shaped these traditions. Mythology more broadly includes Russian folklore as a distinct branch of European mythological thinking. Folk traditions are the broader category of which Russian folklore is a defining regional exemplar.
